Senses.Explanation: The quarters supervisor is the officer responsible for the monks' common quarters. Monastic rules assign this officer the quarters' texts and goods, tea, fuel, cleaning, washing, grooming equipment, doors, boards, and attendance; one rule has the supervisor close the quarters door and report that the assembly has gone to seated dhyana. Records also name individual quarters supervisors as requesters or recipients of funeral rites. The title is an administrative office, not a teaching rank.

Senses.Explanation: Read the move and weigh the ounces names exact, responsive appraisal: seeing what an encounter calls for and measuring the response without excess or shortage. Mi'an Xianjie places it after 'raise one and clarify three' among the powers displayed in a formal hall address. Hongjue Min's questioner uses the pair to open a three-phrase interview, and Feiyin Tongrong makes it the capacity that joins ancient and present in one thought. Shiqi Tongyun says a patch-robed monk must possess it; Fushi Mingfang says the right person naturally does. Hansong Zhicao supplies the limit: even cutting off the ten directions while reading the move and weighing the ounces may still be driving a stake and washing one's feet against a bridge post.

Senses.Note: Two independent records actively use the expression. Baoning Renyong applies it to himself in a compact hall saying; Yi'an Shanzan places it in a verse-like sequence about acting naturally. The inherited Langye exchange appears in the transmission records.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X78/X78n1556.xml). Jianzhong Jingguo Continued Lamp Record (建中靖國續燈錄), Langye Zhiqian of Kaihua on Mount Langye in Chuzhou, an heir of Langye Huijue: when the monk asks what is the person of the realm, the master answers with the headword — hair long, the monastic’s looks ugly.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase presents an unidealized monastic appearance: long hair and ugly looks. Baoning Renyong uses it in a self-descriptive cluster with thin legs, loose sandals, glaring eyes, and poor-looking hands. Yi'an Shanzan places it beside acting naturally—walking when walking, sitting when sitting—and the ordinary response of shutting the door when cold.
